answers.answer: No. SCOPe 2.08 does not support treating these three groups as one homologous superfamily. It unites them only at the fold level, as fold f.21 'Heme-binding four-helical bundle' (sunid 81344, class f, membrane and cell surface proteins), whose core is described as four transmembrane helices in an up-and-down bundle binding one or two hemes between the helices. Beneath that fold SCOPe deliberately keeps three distinct superfamilies: f.21.1 'Transmembrane di-heme cytochromes' (sunid 81342), f.21.2 'Fumarate reductase respiratory complex transmembrane subunits' (sunid 81343), and f.21.3 'Respiratory nitrate reductase 1 gamma chain' (sunid 103501). In SCOPe's hierarchy, homology (common ancestry) is asserted at the superfamily and family levels; a shared fold records only the same core secondary-structure architecture and topology, which can arise by convergence, especially for a simple, generic architecture such as a four-helix transmembrane bundle with heme ligated by histidines between helices. The SCOPe homology section for f.21 explicitly reports homology_implied_by_level = false with the warning that levels above superfamily do not imply homology, whereas each of the three superfamilies carries homology_implied_by_level = true with scope limited to its own superfamily. So members within f.21.1 (e.g. the two di-heme cytochrome families, where SCOPe notes three of the four heme ligands are conserved and both hemes bind similarly but not identically) are treated as homologs of one another, and members within f.21.2 (two families, one with the fold in a single chain and one with the fold built from two chains, e.g. FrdC/FrdD-type subunits) are homologs of one another, but f.21.1 members are not asserted to be homologous to f.21.2 or f.21.3 members. The curators' own comment on f.21.3 shows how carefully this is hedged: the nitrate reductase gamma chain is described as a 'possible link between the two other superfamilies' because it is the functional counterpart of the formate dehydrogenase N gamma subunit (a di-heme cytochrome, f.21.1) yet is structurally closer to the fumarate reductase subunit FrdC (f.21.2). SCOPe still left it as its own superfamily (mapped to Pfam PF02665), i.e. the evidence was judged suggestive but insufficient to merge the superfamilies. Limits: (1) the fold-level grouping must not be used to transfer function, cofactor-ligation details, electron-transfer partners, or quinone-binding sites across superfamilies; (2) a four-helix heme bundle is a low-complexity architecture, so structural similarity alone is weak evidence of descent; (3) the arrangement reflects curation on the structures available in SCOPe 2.08 (f.21.1 and f.21.2 date from SCOP 1.63/1.65-era entries, f.21.3 from the NarGHI structure) and could be revised by newer evidence; (4) to argue for a single homologous superfamily one would need external evidence beyond SCOPe, such as statistically significant sequence or profile-profile (HMM) similarity linking the Pfam families, conserved sequence motifs around the heme-ligating histidines in equivalent positions, shared unusual structural features beyond the generic bundle, or genomic/operon context, and then propose a SCOPe curation change rather than infer it from the shared fold. Within the current release, the correct statement is: same fold (f.21), three separate superfamilies, no SCOPe-asserted homology among the three groups.
